{"id": "679b96a6-1367-47e1-94bc-9a2a71117e20", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_evhcKg745MRN2oaIUmMgX4", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Configure a Direct Connect Classic connection\",\"context\":\"## (Recommended) Step 7: Configure redundant connections\\n\\nTo provide for failover, we recommend that you request and configure two dedicated\\nconnections to AWS, as shown in the following figure. These connections can terminate on\\none or two routers in your network.\\n\\nThere are different configuration choices available when you provision two\\ndedicated connections:\\n\\n* Active/Active (BGP multipath). This is the default configuration, where\\n both connections are active. Direct Connect supports multipathing to multiple\\n virtual interfaces within the same location, and traffic is load-shared\\n between interfaces based on flow. If one connection becomes unavailable, all\\n traffic is routed through the other connection.\\n* Active/Passive (failover). One connection is handling traffic, and the\\n other is on standby. If the active connection becomes unavailable, all traffic\\n is routed through the passive connection. You need to prepend the AS path to the\\n routes on one of your links for that to be the passive link.\\n\\nHow you configure the connections doesn't affect redundancy, but it does affect\\nthe policies that determine how your data is routed over both connections. We recommend\\nthat you configure both connections as active.\\n\\nIf you use a VPN connection for redundancy, ensure that you implement a health check\\nand failover mechanism. If you use either of the following configurations, then you need\\nto check your route table routing to route to the new network interface.\\n\\n* You use your own instances for routing, for example the instance is the\\n firewall.\\n* You use your own instance that terminates a VPN connection.\\n\\nTo achieve high availability, we strongly recommend that you configure connections to\\ndifferent Direct Connect locations.\\n\\nFor more information about Direct Connect resiliency, see Direct Connect Resiliency Recommendations\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I set an Active/Passive Direct Connect connection to AWS?\",\"context\":\"Resolution\\n-----------\\n\\nWhen using Direct Connect to transport production workloads to and from AWS, it's a best practice to use dual Direct Connect connections using different data centers or providers.\\n\\nConfigure the following:\\n\\n* Two routers to terminate the primary and secondary Direct Connect\u00a0connections to avoid a single point of device failure.\\n* A private virtual interface on each of the Direct Connect\u00a0routers that terminate to the same Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).\\n* High availability routing protocols (such as HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP) on two routers to allow local servers to use multiple routers that act as a single virtual router. This configuration helps you to maintain connectivity even if the primary router fails. \\n-or- \\nRun an internal routing protocol (such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) that learns routes from Direct Connect external BGP gateways and distributes prefixes to internal BGP gateways.\\n* Active/Passive (failover). In this scenario, one connection handles traffic, and the other is on standby. If the active connection becomes unavailable, all traffic is routed through the passive connection. You must use Autonomous System (AS) prepending for the routes on one of your links to set it as the passive link.\\n\\nFor more information, see [Configure redundant connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/dev-test-resiliency.html).\\n\\n**Note:** Check your vendor documentation for commands that are specific to your network device\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/active-passive-direct-connect\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How do I set up an Active/Passive Direct Connect connection to AWS?\",\"context\":\"Resolution\\n----------\\n\\n**Note:** It's a best practice to use dual Direct Connect connections through different data centers or providers to transport production workloads to and from AWS.\\n\\nConfigure the following:\\n\\n* Two routers on an on-premises location to terminate the primary and secondary Direct Connect connections to avoid a single point of device failure.\\n* A private VIF on each of the Direct Connect routers that terminate to the same Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).\\n* High availability routing protocols (such as HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP) on two routers. This allows local servers to use multiple routers that act as a single virtual router. This configuration helps maintain connectivity even if the primary router fails. You can also run an internal routing protocol such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).\\n* In an Active/Passive Direct Connect setup (failover), an active connection handles traffic and a passive connection is on standby. If the active connection becomes unavailable, then all traffic must be routed through the passive connection. Use Autonomous System (AS) prepending for the routes on one of your links to set the link as passive.\\n\\n**Note:** Check your vendor documentation for commands that are specific to your network device.\\n\\nFor more information on configuring redundant Direct Connect connections on AWS, see [Configure redundant connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/getting_started.html#RedundantConnections)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-active-passive-connection\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify AWS Direct Connect VIF failover BGP direction requirements in docs"}

{"id": "717aac1d-3834-4410-8003-b3b6c6f2dea3", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Based on AWS's documented guidance, auditing redundant VIFs for failover resilience means checking BGP routing policy in **both directions**, since a failure can hide in either one and only surface during an actual outage:

**1. Outbound advertisements (on-premises → AWS)**
- This is where **AS path prepending** lives, which is how you designate a link as passive in an Active/Passive setup.
- Audit check: confirm the prepend is actually applied on the intended backup VIF, and that it's long enough to lose the route comparison on AWS's side. A missing or too-short prepend means AWS may still prefer the "passive" link — defeating the failover design.

**2. Inbound advertisements (AWS → on-premises)**
- AWS advertises VPC/on-prem-reachable prefixes to you over BGP on each VIF. Your router's local preference / weight / AS path filtering on these inbound routes determines which VIF your traffic actually egresses on.
- Audit check: confirm your router's route selection matches the intended primary/passive roles. It's common for outbound prepending to be configured correctly while inbound policy on the router still prefers the "wrong" VIF — that asymmetry causes real failover surprises.

**Why both matter together:** BGP path selection is independent in each direction. A redundant pair can look correctly configured on paper but fail asymmetrically — e.g., traffic properly fails over outbound but return traffic still tries to come back over the dead link, or vice versa. For Active/Active (BGP multipath) pairs, the check shifts from prepending to confirming multipathing/ECMP is actually enabled and traffic is load-sharing across both VIFs rather than silently pinned to one.

Also worth checking as part of the same audit, per AWS's resiliency recommendations: whether the redundant VIFs terminate at different Direct Connect locations (not just different connections at the same location) — that's a separate failure domain concern from the BGP direction issue but usually gets audited in the same pass.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
